prompt: Which device is foregrounded by repeating the opening words?
distractors: Epistrophe: repetition at the ends of successive clauses.
Antithesis: a contrast between opposing ideas.
definition: Anaphora repeats an opening across successive clauses. Epistrophe repeats an ending. Locate the pattern before naming it.
memory: I need a pen. I need a plan. I need a class that stops hiding ducks in my desk.
memoryJoke:
Lin: Is the duck part of the definition?
Hepting [determined]: The duck is under investigation.
context: Vex wants a chorus that a stadium can join before the second repetition.
intro: Vex [determined]: Our chorus must unite fifty thousand people. Ideally without requiring fifty thousand dictionaries.

lyrics.text: We own the night. We own the noise. We own tomorrow.
lyrics.evidence: We own begins each clause
lyrics.effect: The repeated We own gives fans a predictable entrance and turns the chorus into a claim of collective confidence.
lyrics.reaction: Vex [proud]: Excellent. We have acquired tomorrow. Finance will be delighted.

lyrics.text: Let them stare. Let them doubt. Let them hear us now.
lyrics.evidence: Let them begins each clause
lyrics.effect: The repeated Let them builds a defiant invitation to keep going despite an audience of doubters.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [determined]: I can hear the audience joining the final command.

lyrics.text: Still I stumble. Still I sparkle. Still I take the stage.
lyrics.evidence: Still I begins each clause
lyrics.effect: The repeated Still I makes persistence the pattern, giving anxious listeners a refrain they can claim themselves.
lyrics.reaction: Vex [relieved]: Finally, choreography that includes my actual abilities.

wrongEffect: It proves every audience member already agrees with the singer.
genericEffect: It sounds good, so we do not need to identify any particular wording.
gagText: Vex gives my shoulder one absurdly gentle rubber-duck boop. The duck squeaks as though filing a complaint.
gagLine:
Vex [angry]: THIS IS SERIOUS.
Sora [skeptical]: Then stop delegating discipline to bath equipment.
outro:
Manager [worried]: Six sections left. Our launch countdown has begun.
Lin [skeptical]: Is it measured in minutes?
Manager [embarrassed]: Slides. We could not afford the timer subscription.

prompt: Which device is foregrounded by setting opposing ideas against one another?
distractors: Anaphora: repeated openings across successive clauses.
A simile explicitly comparing two things with like or as.
definition: Antithesis puts contrasting ideas beside each other. Parallel phrasing can make the contrast clearer, but parallel structure alone is not an opposition.
memoryJoke:
Lin [skeptical]: That is also the title of your classroom equipment policy.
Hepting [proud]: A document with range.
context: Sora wants a comeback verse that turns rejection into defiance.
intro: Sora [determined]: The verse needs a turn: what they wanted from us against what we become.

lyrics.text: You wanted silence; I became thunder.
lyrics.evidence: silence contrasts with thunder
lyrics.effect: The contrast turns an attempt to silence the speaker into loud resistance; thunder also supplies a metaphor.
lyrics.reaction:
Vex [excited]: I will become actual thunder.
Sora [worried]: Please leave the electrical panel alone.

lyrics.text: They count our failures; we count our chances.
lyrics.evidence: failures contrasts with chances in matching clauses
lyrics.effect: The balanced contrast reframes the same setbacks as opportunities, inviting fans to adopt the group's resilience.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [worried]: Can we count our invoices next?

lyrics.text: Your palace feels empty; our basement feels alive.
lyrics.evidence: empty palace contrasts with lively basement
lyrics.effect: The contrast makes belonging seem more valuable than status, appealing to listeners who feel overlooked.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [happy]: A room can be small without the life inside it being small.

wrongEffect: It establishes that the contrast is a proven fact about every listener.
genericEffect: It persuades because all parallel sentences contain opposing ideas.
gagText: Vex reaches toward me with a foam pool noodle. It folds around his own elbow before its tip taps my sleeve.
gagLine:
Vex [angry]: FEAR MY AUTHORITY.
Lin [curious]: Your authority appears to be tied in a bow.
outro:
I: The manager advances the countdown slide. The next number is larger.
Manager [determined]: That is a design error. Feel more urgency anyway.

prompt: Which device treats one thing as another rather than describing it literally?
distractors: Epistrophe: the same ending repeated across clauses.
A rhetorical question addressed to the listener.
definition: A metaphor presents one thing as another. Explain what the comparison lets a reader imagine. The comparison is not a literal fact.
memory: My inbox is a swamp. Notice: I do not need to write like a swamp to make the comparison.
memoryJoke:
Lin [worried]: Is that why you have not answered my email?
Hepting [determined]: Rescue operations are ongoing.
context: Sora wants a heartbreak line that makes a feeling concrete without explaining every detail.
intro: Sora [sad]: I want to show the feeling. Vex keeps suggesting that I announce the feeling through a megaphone.

lyrics.text: Your goodbye is a city I still live in.
lyrics.evidence: goodbye becomes a city inhabited by the speaker
lyrics.effect: The place metaphor makes lingering grief feel like an environment the speaker cannot simply leave.
lyrics.reaction:
Vex [confused]: Does this city have affordable rent?
Sora [sad]: Emotionally, no.

lyrics.text: My heart is a nightclub with your name on every door.
lyrics.evidence: the heart becomes a nightclub marked by one person's name
lyrics.effect: The image makes private longing vivid through a familiar social space, suggesting that every route leads back to one person.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [curious]: At least the venue has multiple exits.

lyrics.text: Your promise was a paper umbrella in the rain.
lyrics.evidence: the promise becomes an inadequate umbrella
lyrics.effect: The fragile protection suggests that the promise failed when needed, giving disappointment a concrete image.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [determined]: A promise that looked useful until the weather changed. That hurts.

wrongEffect: It supplies scientific evidence that feelings literally become physical objects.
genericEffect: It appeals only because all metaphors mean the same thing: love.
gagText: Vex presents the rubber duck directly toward me, as if its painted eyes can extract an answer. It gives my sleeve a squeaky tap.
gagLine:
Vex [determined]: THE DUCK KNOWS.
Lin [skeptical]: Then why is it not enrolled in AP Language?
outro:
Sora [curious]: You keep making us say what the image does, not just what it is called.
I: Yes. The device name is the doorway. We still have to enter the room.

prompt: Which device deliberately exaggerates the amount or scale?
distractors: A concession acknowledging a reasonable opposing point.
definition: Hyperbole deliberately stretches scale for an effect. In a lyric, an impossible quantity can convey feeling without pretending to be a measured fact.
memory: I have explained this a billion times. Not a verified statistic. A very tired teacher's emphasis.
memoryJoke:
Lin [curious]: Would a million still count?
Hepting [worried]: Please do not turn this into a spreadsheet.
context: Vex wants recognisable, ridiculous heartbreak for listeners who have waited for a reply.
intro:
Vex [pleading]: I need a line that says I am normal about this breakup.
Sora [skeptical]: Your draft contains nine exclamation marks and a weather warning.

lyrics.text: I checked my phone a million times before the chorus.
lyrics.evidence: a million checks within one short musical interval
lyrics.effect: The impossible frequency makes anxious checking recognisable through comic exaggeration.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [worried]: Your screen-time report has requested a lawyer.

lyrics.text: I cried enough to put the moon underwater.
lyrics.evidence: tears impossibly flooding as high as the moon
lyrics.effect: The impossible scale makes grief extravagantly large, inviting listeners to enjoy the melodrama rather than calculate the water.
lyrics.reaction: Vex [proud]: Finally, an affordable concept for the music video.

lyrics.text: I would cross a thousand galaxies for one unread message.
lyrics.evidence: vast travel exchanged for a tiny and disappointing reward
lyrics.effect: The exaggerated effort turns longing into comic excess, especially beside the anticlimax of an unread message.
lyrics.reaction:
Sora [skeptical]: Or you could put the phone down.
Vex [shocked]: We are writing fiction, Sora.

wrongEffect: It proves the singer's literal claim by supplying a large number.
genericEffect: It must make every listener sad because exaggeration has only one possible effect.
gagText: The foam noodle droops against my shoulder. Vex tries to lift it dramatically and nearly tickles his own ear.
gagLine:
Vex [angry]: THIS WILL BE THE MOST TERRIFYING MOMENT IN ALL HUMAN HISTORY.
Lin [curious]: Was that our next example?
outro:
Manager [worried]: Three sections left. The livestream waiting room is open.
Sora [worried]: How many viewers?
Manager [embarrassed]: One. My mother. She has already asked us to stand up straight.

prompt: In this song context, which device asks in order to challenge or provoke thought rather than obtain an answer?
distractors: Hypophora: asking a question and then immediately answering it.
Anaphora: repeated openings across successive clauses.
definition: A rhetorical question does something beyond requesting information. Context matters: the same words could become a genuine question in an interview. Hypophora supplies the speaker's own answer.
memory: Who needs another worksheet? In this memory, I am protesting the pile, not conducting a survey.
memoryJoke:
Lin [happy]: I vote no.
Hepting [skeptical]: That response was suspiciously prepared.
context: The bridge addresses a doubting listener; the singer leaves the question hanging rather than answering it.
intro: Sora [determined]: This bridge should make a doubter confront something. No customer-service reply form.

lyrics.text: If we meant nothing, why are you still singing?
lyrics.evidence: the unanswered question challenges the claim that the relationship meant nothing
lyrics.effect: It uses the listener's continued singing as a challenge to their denial, inviting them to reconsider their attachment.
lyrics.reaction: Vex [determined]: The audience has been cross-examined. In harmony.

lyrics.text: Who said a broken voice cannot fill a stadium?
lyrics.evidence: the question challenges an assumed limit without seeking a named person
lyrics.effect: It pushes back against exclusion and invites imperfect singers to imagine belonging in a huge shared space.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [happy]: That one lets people sing before they feel perfect.

lyrics.text: How can you call this goodbye when you know every word?
lyrics.evidence: the unanswered challenge contrasts departure with remembered lyrics
lyrics.effect: It invites the listener to notice a tension between claiming to leave and still knowing the shared song.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [worried]: Please do not make goodbye legally impossible. We need the studio by nine.

wrongEffect: It requires every concertgoer to submit a factual written answer.
genericEffect: It is automatically hypophora because any question answers itself.
gagText: Vex gently boops my sleeve with the duck, then holds it to his ear as if waiting for expert advice.
gagLine:
Vex [angry]: DO YOU THINK THIS IS A GAME?
Lin [curious]: Are you requesting information, or demonstrating the device?
Vex [confused]: I require a moment.
outro:
Sora [curious]: Earlier we repeated an opening. Now we leave an unanswered challenge. Different tools, different reasons to use them.
I: The manager has begun rehearsing our apology in the corner.

prompt: Which device is foregrounded by the repeated consonant sound near the starts of words?
distractors: Rhyme: matching sounds at word endings.
definition: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, often at word beginnings. Listen to sounds, not just spelling. A sound pattern can support a tone, but it does not dictate one universal emotion.
memory: Clever kittens conquer chaos. The repeated k sound crosses the different spellings c and k.
memoryJoke:
Lin [curious]: Have the kittens submitted a plan?
Hepting [worried]: They have eaten the plan.
context: Sora wants a line whose sound is noticeable and whose words still serve its meaning.
intro: Sora [determined]: Vex has written seventeen words beginning with B. It is less a lyric than a malfunctioning printer.

lyrics.text: Silk smiles sell beautiful lies.
lyrics.evidence: Silk, smiles and sell repeat the s sound
lyrics.effect: The s pattern links smooth appearance with deception; in these words it can support a sleek, suspicious tone.
lyrics.reaction: Vex [skeptical]: My smile objects to being investigated.

lyrics.text: Bright beats break the bedroom gloom.
lyrics.evidence: Bright, beats, break and bedroom repeat the b sound
lyrics.effect: The repeated b gives the phrase an audible pattern that can reinforce its energetic movement out of gloom.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [happy]: The sound has a job. It is not just wearing a costume.

lyrics.text: Cold coffee keeps your company.
lyrics.evidence: Cold, coffee, keeps and company repeat the k sound
lyrics.effect: The repeated k links the small details of lonely routine into a compact, noticeable phrase.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [sad]: That is the first lyric to represent my working conditions.

wrongEffect: The repeated consonant guarantees the same emotion for every audience.
genericEffect: It must be rhyme because any repeated sound occurs at a word ending.
gagText: Vex advances with the foam noodle. It brushes my sleeve, then flops across his own face like a pink moustache.
gagLine:
Vex [angry]: PERFECTLY PROFESSIONAL PUNISHMENT.
Lin [laughing]: Your prop appears to support your point.
outro:
Manager [worried]: Final section. The launch button is now pulsating.
Sora [skeptical]: You are moving the mouse over it.
Manager [determined]: I am creating stakes.

prompt: In this context of obvious frustration, which device makes the literal praise mean its opposite?
distractors: A literal compliment sincerely celebrating the situation.
Anaphora: the same opening repeated in successive clauses.
definition: Verbal irony can use praise to convey criticism when context reverses the literal meaning. A ridiculous situation alone is not enough. Ask what the speaker intends.
memory: Wonderful. The projector has frozen for the third time. My words praise it; my evident frustration does not.
memoryJoke:
Lin [skeptical]: Is your earlier THIS IS SERIOUS joke automatically verbal irony?
Hepting [determined]: No. If Vex means it sincerely, the comic mismatch is not verbal irony. Intention and context matter.
context: The singer is openly frustrated, not sincerely pleased. Deliver each line with that context in mind.
intro:
Vex [proud]: The last line must communicate that I am completely fine.
Sora [skeptical]: You have labelled the folder ABSOLUTELY NOT FINE.

lyrics.text: Perfect timing—you left on my birthday.
lyrics.evidence: Perfect praises timing that the hurt singer plainly resents
lyrics.effect: The reversal turns apparent praise into a bitter complaint, inviting listeners to recognise the speaker's hurt beneath controlled wording.
lyrics.reaction: Manager [worried]: We should clarify that leaving on birthdays is not company policy.

lyrics.text: How thoughtful—you forgot my name again.
lyrics.evidence: thoughtful describes behaviour the speaker experiences as thoughtless
lyrics.effect: The ironic compliment criticises repeated neglect while allowing the singer to sound controlled rather than openly pleading.
lyrics.reaction: Sora [sad]: The again makes the neglect a pattern.

lyrics.text: What a generous gift: another excuse.
lyrics.evidence: generous gift praises an excuse the speaker does not welcome
lyrics.effect: The reversal exposes an excuse as an inadequate substitute for care, inviting the listener to share the criticism.
lyrics.reaction:
Vex [confused]: Should I keep the receipt?
Sora [determined]: Especially for the excuse.

wrongEffect: It sincerely thanks the other person; the frustrated context is irrelevant.
genericEffect: It is irony only because any unhappy event automatically reverses the meaning of words.
gagText: Vex offers the duck its final intimidating entrance. Its squeak is so small that he apologises to it.
gagLine:
Vex [worried]: We rehearsed this, Mr. Quackers.
Lin [skeptical]: A flawless demonstration of overwhelming power.
Sora [curious]: That reply, with this context, is verbal irony.
outro:
Manager [shocked]: The stream is live.
Vex [shocked]: We have not rehearsed.
Manager [determined]: Then it will look spontaneous.
I: The door clicks open. Apparently the key was under the emergency choreography mat.
